In the modern large Chinese orchestra it belongs to the string section along with the erhu, zhonghu, banhu, cello and double bass. Listen to pieces such as 《步步高》 (“Rising Step by Step”) and 《平湖秋月》 (“Calm Lake, Autumn Moon”) to hear its bright, light timbre and its smaller volume.

Its soundbox is smaller and its front is covered with python skin, so its overall volume is on the quiet side; traditionally the soundbox is held between the knees, unlike most huqin, which rest on the left thigh. It leads in Cantonese music and Cantonese opera, and it belongs to the string section of the modern large Chinese orchestra.

It was created in the 1920s by the musician and composer Lü Wencheng (1898–1981) for Cantonese music and Cantonese opera, and became the leading instrument of Cantonese music and of Cantonese opera orchestras. At first a regional instrument found only in Cantonese music, it was later taken into the string section of the modern large Chinese orchestra in various forms, alongside the erhu, zhonghu, banhu, cello and double bass.

The gaohu (also called yuehu) is a Chinese bowed chordophone of the huqin family, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.312. It was developed in the 1920s from the erhu by the musician and composer Lü Wencheng, is used in Cantonese music and Cantonese opera bands, and is their leading instrument. Its construction is close to the erhu's: a smaller soundbox, mostly round, two strings, a python-skin front, and tuning a fourth above the erhu at G4 and D5; traditionally the soundbox is held between the knees. In the modern large Chinese orchestra it is also used as a member of the string section.
